story.title: Mike Johnson Steps Down as House Republican Leader Following GOP Losses
story.summary: House Speaker Mike Johnson announced he will not continue as the Republican leader in the upcoming Congress after the party's significant losses in the recent elections. This decision was communicated to his staff during a phone call, marking a notable shift in House Republican leadership as they prepare for the new session.

explore_lenses.label: What actually changes when Johnson steps aside?
explore_lenses.title: The GOP loses its designated House leader
explore_lenses.summary: Johnson is declining to seek the House Republican leadership post for the next Congress, not merely relinquishing the speakership. Because Democrats won House control, the post at stake is minority leader rather than speaker.

claims.text: Johnson told staff he will not run for House minority leader, according to reporting based on a person familiar with his plans.

The Speaker is chosen by the full House and leads its majority party, while party delegations separately select their own leaders; a Republican leader in the next Congress would therefore lead the minority rather than preside as Speaker.
Johnson said after Democrats claimed the majority that Republicans would continue fighting what he characterized as an incoming Democratic House majority led by 'radical and extreme leftists.'

points: Johnson told staff he will not run for House minority leader, according to reporting based on a person familiar with his plans.

Johnson said after Democrats claimed the majority that Republicans would continue fighting what he characterized as an incoming Democratic House majority led by 'radical and extreme leftists.'
explore_lenses.uncertainty_note: The reporting establishes that Johnson will not seek the party-leader post; it does not, by itself, settle his longer-term plans in Congress.

explore_lenses.label: Who could replace Johnson as House GOP leader?
explore_lenses.title: Scalise and Jordan are early contenders
explore_lenses.summary: Johnson’s departure opens an internal Republican leadership race. Reporting identifies Majority Leader Steve Scalise and Judiciary Committee Chair Jim Jordan as possible successors, but the conference has not yet voted.

claims.text: Roll Call reported that Scalise and Jordan had expressed interest in the minority-leader role.
Axios reported that Johnson’s exit was expected to trigger a potentially contentious contest, with Scalise and Jordan floated as successors.
The House Clerk identifies Scalise as the current majority leader, and the House Republican membership page identifies Jordan as Judiciary Committee chair.

explore_lenses.label: What happens next procedurally?
explore_lenses.title: Republicans choose a leader before Congress convenes
explore_lenses.summary: The Republican Conference is expected to select its leader internally, while the full House will choose the next Speaker after the new Congress begins. These are separate votes with different electorates.

claims.text: Roll Call reported that House Republicans were set to hold leadership elections the following week.

Republican Conference rules provide for contested leadership elections by secret ballot, with successive ballots eliminating the lowest-finishing candidate until someone wins a majority when more than two candidates run.
A new Congress begins at noon on January 3 of each odd-numbered year unless Congress sets another date; the next Congress is therefore scheduled to begin January 3, 2027.
The minority leader will be selected by Republican members, whereas the Speaker will be elected by the entire House.

story_report.summary: Mike Johnson told staff on a phone call that he will not seek another term as House Republican leader after Republicans suffered a significant electoral defeat and Democrats claimed the House majority. His decision means House Republicans will need to choose a minority leader for the next Congress rather than retain Johnson at the head of their conference. The reporting establishes his decision not to seek the leadership post but does not determine his longer-term plans in Congress.

sections.heading: House Leadership Roles Differ
sections.body: The Speaker is elected by the full House and leads the chamber’s majority party, while each party’s members separately select their own leaders. Because Democrats have claimed the majority, the Republican selected to succeed Johnson as party leader would serve as minority leader rather than preside as Speaker. Republican members, not the full House, will choose that minority leader.

sections.heading: Republicans Face Leadership Contest
sections.body: Roll Call reported that House Republicans were set to hold leadership elections the following week. It reported that Steve Scalise and Jim Jordan had expressed interest in the minority-leader role; the House Clerk identifies Scalise as majority leader, while the House Republican membership page identifies Jordan as Judiciary Committee chair. Under conference rules, contested leadership elections are decided by secret ballot, with successive ballots eliminating the lowest-finishing candidate until a majority winner emerges when more than two candidates run.

unresolved.text: The reporting reviewed did not establish the final candidate field, the outcome or final date of the Republican Conference leadership election, and the conference could alter its internal rules or schedule.
Johnson’s longer-term plans in Congress were not settled by the reporting that established he would not seek the party-leader post.

related_stories.title: Democrats Gain Control of Congress in Midterm Elections
related_stories.summary: In a significant shift during the 2026 midterm elections, Democrats have regained control of both the House and Senate, marking their first full control of Congress since 2023. This outcome allows them to block President Trump's nominees and influence his agenda. The election results reflect a broader dissatisfaction with Trump's leadership, particularly in light of ongoing issues such as the Iran war.

related_stories.title: Troy Jackson Secures Senate Seat in Maine, Defeating Susan Collins
related_stories.summary: Democrat Troy Jackson has won the U.S. Senate race in Maine, defeating incumbent Republican Senator Susan Collins. Jackson, a former state Senate president and logger, became the Democratic nominee after Graham Platner withdrew from the race in July. His victory is seen as a significant gain for the Democratic Party in the midterm elections.
